seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p:
I owe you an apology for my delay in answering your letter and in acknowledging receipt of
Poetry and of your little volume of translations . My sister’s marriage, which took place here the day before yesterday, caused a good deal of confusion in my family and I had no time to enjoy your verses. I have read your book with much pleasure and should like very much to speak with you about it. I hope I shall soon have that pleasure. Meanwhile whenever you can I hope you will send me a photograph. I intend to have some done for it is ten or twelve years since I had a photograph done, except for a snapshot made in a hurry last summer. There seems to be a new and most complicated tangle about an American edition of Dubliners . Grant Richards writes to say that he knows nothing of it and is writing at once to New York to find out. The letter of the editor of The Smart Set alludes plainly to an American edition, already published. I have ceded to Mr Pinker the disposal of dramatic rights of my play Exiles and, if Grant Richards does not publish the novel, also the book rights of it. In any case whether Grant Richards accept or refuse I wish that Mr Pinker act as my agent – a post till now occupied with great success by you – and if you see him I hope you will tell him so.

div.note: This letter, which appears clearly dated “19 April 1915” in JJ’s hand, raises a question about the date of his sister Eileen’s wedding in Trieste (see below). Scholars typically state that a wedding took place on 12 April 1915, a Monday. But JJ in this letter reports that the wedding took place “the day before yesterday,” thus on 17 April, a Saturday. Unless the 12 April consensus is incorrect, it seems possible that there were two ceremonies, perhaps an initial, private one for the couple, and a second one for the family.
For JJ’s use of this wartime mailing address, see JJ to Pound, 3 April 1915, notes.

JJ has received copies of the magazine Poetry and Pound’s volume of verse, Cathay, as promised by Pound in his letter to JJ of ca. 29 March 1915 (Pound/Joyce 33-34). See JJ to Pound, 3 April 1915, notes.

Eileen Isabella Joyce (1889-1963) had traveled with her brother JJ in January 1910 from Dublin to Trieste, where she joined a ménage that included, besides JJ, his partner Nora Barnacle, their children Giorgio and Lucia, his sister Eva, and intermittently his brother Stanislaus. In April 1914, Eileen became engaged to Frantisek (Frank) Schaurek, a Czech bank cashier in Trieste who had been JJ’s pupil. They were married in April 1915 in the cathedral of San Giusto, Trieste, with JJ acting as best man. The couple spent the war years in Prague and named their daughters Bozena Berta (Beatrice Bertha) and Eleanora (Nora), for Nora Barnacle and the chief female characters in Exiles.
For the photographs Pound sent to JJ, see JJ to Pound, 3 April 1915, notes.

Grant Richards, English publisher of Dubliners (1914), wrote JJ on 12 April 1915 to say that no American edition of Dubliners had been arranged for. He wrote JJ again on 26 April 1915 that “[t]here has been no American edition of ‘Dubliners.’ Pirates in America are not now active” (Robert Scholes, “Grant Richard to James Joyce,” Studies in Bibliography, vol. 16 [1963]: 156-57). JJ’s concern was partly, as he indicated in a letter to Richards dated 19 April 1915, that, because Richards had not arranged for prompt publication of Dubliners as a book in the United States, the work’s U.S. copyright might have been (as indeed it was) lost (LII 339). In his 26 April letter, Richards added, unconsolingly, that “[i]n any case a book like ‘Dubliners’ is unlikely to have been pirated” (Scholes, 157). Dubliners was published as a book in America in late 1916 by B.W. Huebsch, most likely the person JJ here says Richards is writing to in New York.

note.p: The American journalist and cultural critic H.L. Mencken (1880-1956) coedited the New York literary magazine The Smart Set with George Jean Nathan (1882-1958) from 1914 to 1924. The magazine published important avant-garde authors both before and during Mencken’s tenure. Mencken’s letter to JJ of 3 March 1915 had created the misimpression that an American edition of Dubliners was being published, a confusion that Mencken sought to clear up in his 20 April 1915 letter to JJ, noting that B.W. Huebsch had planned to bring out the book at around this time but had been delayed (LI 79).

In early 1914, Pound had offered The Smart Set three stories from Dubliners: “An Encounter,” “The Boarding House,” and “A Little Cloud.” He had hoped that the magazine’s progressive and ambitious editor, Willard Huntington Wright (1888-1939), would accept the stories, even though he told JJ, with damningly faint praise, that Wright “regards himself as the sane normal and practical male” but “has exactly twice as much sense as the common american editor, a sort of double zero leaning toward the infinitesimal” (LII 327). The submitted stories apparently arrived and were rejected after Wright had left The Smart Set in the wake of financial turmoil, and before Mencken and Nathan were installed as the new editors. In early March 1915, Mencken wrote JJ that The Smart Set was publishing two of the stories – “The Boarding House” and “A Little Cloud” – in The Smart Set, vol. 46, no. 1 (May 1915): 93-97, 129-36. He sent two copies of this number to JJ in April 1915 (LI 77-78, 79).

div.note: For JJ’s new agent, J.B. Pinker, and the publication of JJ’s novel, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, and his play, Exiles, see JJ to Pound, 3 April 1915, notes.
